findings.reason: lock() and try_lock() take `self.storage.lock()`, which is the `&Mutex` every partition of the device shares. The new test, which holds `factory.lock()` and then sees `settings.try_lock()` fail, shows the device-wide scope. The doc comment only says the mutex is held for the guard's lifetime. Lowered P3 from medium to low: the code behaves as an ordinary non-reentrant mutex, so the gap is documentation.
findings.claim: A PartitionGuard holds the mutex shared by the whole device, so it blocks every partition on that device. If the same task then awaits another Partition operation, it deadlocks. The docs don't mention either point.
findings.evidence: `lock()` returns a guard that holds `self.storage.lock().await`. Every partition shares that `&Mutex<M, F>` (test/mod.rs map). The test at test/bdd.rs:128-132 confirms that holding `factory.lock()` makes `settings.try_lock()` fail. The doc comment only says 'The underlying mutex is held for the lifetime of this guard'. README.md:76 describes the Mutex but not the new lock API.

members.claim: Holding a PartitionGuard blocks every other partition on the same device, because they all share one mutex. If a task awaits any Partition operation (or `lock()` on another partition) while holding a guard, it waits forever, and neither the docs nor the README warn about this.

members.claim: `lock()` and `try_lock()` lock the mutex for the whole device, which every partition from the same `PartitionManager` shares. A `PartitionGuard` therefore blocks every other partition on the device, not just this one; the tests confirm this, since holding `factory.lock()` makes `settings.try_lock()` fail. The docs say the guard gives exclusive access to "a partition's underlying storage" and don't warn about this. If a task holds a guard and then calls a normal `Partition` method (on this or any other partition of the device) in the same task, it deadlocks forever. That is the same kind of deadlock this PR is meant to prevent. Document the device-wide scope and the re-entrancy hazard clearly.

findings.reason: The guard's read/write/erase methods are async (they implement embedded-storage-async and BlockDevice), so a synchronous context can't call them without an executor. The packet has no story that says panic handlers are the target, so I can't tell whether this misses the goal. Low: it is an API-design point.
findings.claim: try_lock() can't serve the panic-handler use case, because every operation on the guard is async.
findings.evidence: The PR's motivation is panic handlers, but `try_lock()` doesn't really deliver that. Every operation on the returned guard (`read`/`write`/`erase`) is `async`, and a `#[panic_handler]` or other sync context can't await without its own executor or block_on. Also, in typical no_std builds (panic=abort / panic-probe), a panicking task never releases the lock, so try_lock will always fail there. The documentation should say what the supported use case is, or a blocking API should be provided, so users don't build crash-logging on an assumption that doesn't hold.
